{{Short description|Theorem}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''equioscillation theorem''' concerns the [[Approximation theory|approximation]] of [[continuous function]]s using [[polynomial]]s when the merit function is the maximum difference ([[uniform norm]]). Its discovery is attributed to [[Pafnuty Chebyshev|Chebyshev]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Golomb |first=Michael |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DbnPAAAAMAAJ |title=Lectures on Theory of Approximation |year=1962}}</ref>

== Statement ==
Let <math>f</math> be a continuous function from <math>[a,b]</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. Among all the polynomials of degree <math>\le n</math>, the polynomial <math>g</math> minimizes the uniform norm of the difference <math> \| f - g \| _\infty </math> if and only if there are <math>n+2</math> points <math>a \le x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_{n+1} \le b</math> such that <math>f(x_i) - g(x_i) = \sigma (-1)^i \| f - g \|_\infty</math> where <math>\sigma</math> is either -1 or +1.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Notes on how to prove Chebyshev's equioscillation theorem |url=http://www.math.uiowa.edu/~jeichhol/qual%20prep/Notes/cheb-equiosc-thm_2007.pdf |access-date=2022-04-22 |website= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110702221651/http://www.math.uiowa.edu/~jeichhol/qual%20prep/Notes/cheb-equiosc-thm_2007.pdf |archive-date=2 July 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

That is, the polynomial <math> g </math> oscillates above and below <math> f </math> at the interpolation points, and does so to the same degree.

== Proof ==
Let us define the ''equioscillation'' condition as the condition in the theorem statement, that is, the condition that there exists <math> n+2 </math> ordered points in the interval such that the difference <math> f(x_i) - g(x_i) </math> alternates in sign and is equal in magnitude to the uniform-norm of <math> f(x) - g(x) </math>.

We need to prove that this condition is 'sufficient' for the polynomial <math> g </math> being the best uniform approximation to <math> f </math>, and we need to prove that this condition is 'necessary' for a polynomial to be the best uniform approximation. 
=== Sufficiency ===
Assume by contradiction that a polynomial <math> p(x) </math> of degree less than or equal to <math>n</math> existed that provides a uniformly better approximation to <math> f </math>, which means that <math> \| f - p \|_\infty < \| f - g \|_\infty </math>. Then the polynomial 
:<math> h(x) = g(x) - p(x) = (g(x) - f(x)) - (p(x) - f(x)) </math>
is also of degree less than or equal to <math>n</math>. However, for every <math> x_i </math> of the <math> n+2 </math> points <math> x_0, x_1, ..., x_{n+1} </math>, we know that <math> | p(x_i) - f(x_i) | < | g(x) - f(x) | </math> because <math> |p(x_i) - f(x_i)| \le \| f - p \|_\infty </math> and <math> \| f - p ||_\infty < \| f - g \|_\infty </math> (since <math> p </math> is a better approximation than <math> g </math>). 

Therefore, <math> h(x_i) = (g(x_i) - f(x_i)) - (p(x_i) - f(x_i)) </math> will have the same sign as <math> g(x_i) - f(x_i) </math> (because the second term has a smaller magnitude than the first). Thus, <math> h(x_i) </math> will also alternate sign on these <math> n+2 </math> points, and thus have at least <math> n+1 </math> roots. However, since <math> h </math> is a 'polynomial' of at most degree <math> n </math>, it should only have at most <math> n </math> roots. This is a contradiction.

=== Necessity ===
Given a polynomial <math> g </math>, let us define <math> M = \|f(x) - g(x) \|_\infty </math>. 
We will call a point <math> x </math> an ''upper point'' if <math> f(x) - g(x) = M </math> and a ''lower point'' if it equals <math> -M </math> instead. 

Define an ''alternating set'' (given polynomial <math> g </math> and function <math> f </math>) to be a set of ordered points <math> x_0, ... x_n </math> in <math> [a,b] </math> such that for every point <math> x_i </math> in the alternating set, we have <math> f(x_i) - g(x_i) = \sigma (-1)^i M </math>, where <math> \sigma </math> equals <math>1</math> or <math>-1</math> as before.

Define a ''sectioned alternating set'' to be an alternating set <math> x_0, ... x_n </math> along with nonempty closed intervals <math> I_0, ... I_n </math> called ''sections'' such that 
1. the sections partition <math> [a,b] </math> (meaning that the union of the sections is the whole interval, and the intersection of any two sections is either empty or a single common endpoint)
2. For every <math> i </math>, the <math>i</math>th alternating point <math> x_i</math> is in the <math> i</math>th section <math> I_i </math> 
3. If <math> x_i </math> is an upper point, then <math> I_i </math> contains no lower points. Likewise, if <math> x_i </math> is a lower point, then <math> I_i </math> contains no upper points.
 
Given an approximating polynomial <math> g </math> that does not satisfy the equioscillation condition, it is possible to show that the polynomial will have a two point alternating set. This alternating set can then be expanded to a sectioned alternating set. We can then use this sectioned alternating set to improve the approximation, unless the sectioned alternating set has more than <math> n+2 </math> points in which case our improvement cannot be guaranteed to still be a polynomial of degree at most <math> n </math> {{clarify|reason=Explain the missing steps of this proof.|date=July 2025}}

== Variants ==
The equioscillation theorem is also valid when polynomials are replaced by rational functions: among all rational functions whose numerator has degree <math>\le n</math> and denominator has degree <math>\le m</math>,  the [[rational function]] <math>g = p/q</math>, with <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> being relatively prime polynomials of degree <math>n-\nu</math> and <math>m-\mu</math>, minimizes the uniform norm of the difference <math> \| f - g \| _\infty </math> if and only if there are <math>m + n + 2 - \min\{\mu,\nu\}</math> points <math>a \le x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_{m+n+1 - \min\{\mu, \nu\}} \le b</math> such that <math>f(x_i) - g(x_i) = \sigma (-1)^i \| f - g \|_\infty</math> where <math>\sigma</math> is either -1 or +1.<ref name=":0" />

== Algorithms ==
Several [[minimax approximation algorithm]]s are available, the most common being the [[Remez algorithm]].
